primitives.verbatim_quote: Market-clearing probability (binary): m = Σ pibi / (1 - Σ piwi).
primitives.assumptions: Fair market odds, zero-sum bankrolls, fixed model probabilities.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When denominator approaches zero due to extreme win share accumulation.

primitives.name: Kelly Wager Fraction
primitives.verbatim_quote: Equations & assumptions Kelly with existing bets: f = p - ((1-p)/o)(1 + w/b), where w = win shares, b = bankroll.
primitives.assumptions: Fair odds, Kelly bettor maximizing expected log wealth, zero-sum dynamics.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When odds approach infinity or negative values, or when win shares dominate bankroll.

layer2.mapping: Used in GSE to size model bets and adjust weights in real-time during event evolution.
layer2.telemetry: Dynamic bet sizing factor per model per event.

primitives.name: Credibility Vector
primitives.verbatim_quote: Market-clearing multinomial odds: m is the eigenvector of pwT with eigenvalue 1 (PageRank analogy; credibility vector c = wTm is eigenvector of the self-evaluating matrix S = wTp).
primitives.latex: c = w^T m \text{ where } m \text{ is eigenvector of } pw^T \text{ with eigenvalue 1}
primitives.assumptions: Multinomial outcomes, PageRank-style convergence, stable model interactions.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When matrix S becomes singular or eigenvalues diverge.

layer2.mapping: Represents GSE's dynamic model confidence vector derived from betting behavior.

Sequential updates occur through iterative computation of market-clearing probabilities, which aggregate individual model estimates into a synthetic consensus. The Kelly wager fraction determines how much capital each model allocates per event, enabling real-time model reweighting. This process inherently evaluates models not just on final accuracy but on temporal consistency and responsiveness. The eigenstructure of the win-share matrix provides a principled way to derive credibility vectors, aligning with PageRank’s iterative convergence. Failure modes arise when models produce extreme win shares or when odds deviate from fairness, leading to numerical instability in the market-clearing equations.
